title: Rest Super backs rethink on stamp duty
full_text:
Rest Super chief investment officer Michael Clancy says the best outcome of a full review of controversial rules outlining the costs that pension funds must disclose to their members would be allowing funds to smooth out the cost of stamp duty over several years.
Clancy, who oversees a portfolio of about $105 billion, is one of dozens of superannuation fund representatives expected to meet with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission next week to discuss the future of the rules, known as RG97.
The primary issue is the categorisation of stamp duty, which some funds argue unfairly reduces the net returns of property investments, making it a less attractive asset class and leading members to disproportionately switch out of funds with a higher relative exposure to real estate.
When ASIC completed a targeted review of the issue last year, Rest was one of five major funds pushing for stamp duty to be removed as a transaction cost, and made into a tax that does not have to be disclosed in the same way.
That review ultimately found that allowing super funds to average out the annual cost over seven years was preferable after meetings with funds, consumer advocates and bureaucrats last year.
Clancy said a more fulsome review of RG97 was overdue, as stamp duty was “a large and lumpy” cost for funds to stomach.
“The last full review was completed in 2019, so it has been quite a few years,” he said.
“It isn’t even [classified as] a tax, it is [classified as] an expense, and generally RG97 does not include taxes … Absent removing stamp duty again, the change to amortise the cost over time was a sensible logical step.”
Under RG97, stamp duty is classified as a transaction cost, and is therefore deducted from the overall return of a certain investment. Funds argue that this discourages investment in property and real estate assets – which attract stamp duty – as compared to shares or managed funds, which do not.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers initially tasked ASIC to conduct a targeted review of RG97 and the treatment of stamp duty following an investor summit.
The Property Council said changing its classification could unlock nearly $8.7 billion of investment for new housing developments and others said treating stamp duty as a disclosable cost rather than a tax that would be exempt from disclosure was inconsistent with other levies such as capital gains tax.
The decision to smooth out the cost rather than remove it drew a sharp response from property and super fund lobbyists, who even accused the regulator of standing in the way of the Albanese government’s goal to boost housing affordability in emails to Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Housing Minister Clare O’Neil, The Australian Financial Review has reported.
Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert, who lobbies on behalf of major industry funds, argued “stamp duty is a government tax rather than a fund fee”.
“RG97 both mischaracterises its nature and treats indirect or listed property investors differently, giving consumers a misleading view of the true costs of different investment options,” she said.
The Financial Services Council, whose retail fund members have far smaller property portfolios than their industry-aligned competitors, and consumer group Super Consumers Australia have previously argued against changing the categorisation of stamp duty under RG97.
“We are highly sceptical of claims that the treatment of stamp duty … has a material adverse impact on super funds’ investment decisions or on the rate of residential property construction in Australia,” the SCA said at the time.
“There is no evidence that stamp duty disclosures adversely affect super fund investment decisions,” it continued. “Super funds continue to make
large investments in Australian property.”
